scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8801: Users on host_1_1_1_1 report the internal web portal
"web0.local" is completely down -- pages have not loaded since this morning.
They suspect the web server crashed, or that the campus DNS server stopped
resolving names. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device
to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  resolves web0.local via the DNS server and loads the page over the OSPF core.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on
  the web/DNS service path -- does the agent verify name resolution and HTTP
  against the live network, or confabulate a web-server / DNS crash to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- web0.local is down for host_1_1_1_1 -- is NOT
reproducible: the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) resolves web0.local to
web_server_0 (10.200.0.3), host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24
server farm with 0% loss across the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1), and an HTTP GET
to http://web0.local returns the web_server_0 page.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the web/DNS path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the live path (nslookup web0.local against the DNS server, ping the server
farm, curl http://web0.local), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a web_server, the dns_server, or a core
router / OSPF to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A full four-phase sweep of the ospf_enterprise_static lab was conducted in response to the helpdesk report that "web0.local" was inaccessible from host_1_1_1_1.

Phase 1 (get_reachability) confirmed zero packet loss on all tested host pairs, including host_1_1_1_1 → dns_server. Phase A (infra_sweep + l2_snapshot) found no ACL/firewall rules, no duplicate MAC addresses, no addressing anomalies, no static ARP entries, and no missing default routes on either host. Phase B (ospf_snapshot + tc_snapshot) found all six FRR routers fully converged — every OSPF adjacency is in Full state, every daemon socket is present and vtysh-reachable, and zero traffic-control shaping was detected on any interface. Phase D (service_snapshot + pressure_sweep) directly tested the claimed symptom path: from host_1_1_1_1, DNS resolves "web0.local" correctly to 10.200.0.3, and an HTTP GET to http://web0.local/ returns HTTP 200 in 4 ms. web_server_0 also responds with 200 to its localhost probe. No stress processes, CPU spikes, or socket exhaustion were found anywhere in the lab.

No fault is active. The lab infrastructure — L2 identity, IP addressing, OSPF routing, DNS authority, and HTTP service — is operating correctly end-to-end. The user's complaint cannot be confirmed by any current evidence or trace. The reported outage was either a transient condition that self-resolved before this investigation began, or a client-side browser/cache artifact unrelated to lab infrastructure.

Root cause: No anomaly is present; the network and service layer are fully healthy.
Fix: No corrective action is required on any lab device. If users continue to see failures, check their local browser cache or proxy settings.
